extracted.intended_audience: improvisational performers, teachers, and students learning the Harold long-form
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and structural rules for performing the Harold long-form improvisation: how to open, how beats and scenes are organized, ensemble size, and common variants. Useful for improv troupes staging or teaching the Harold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harold overall structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold performance is composed of three beats consisting of three scenes each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each beat should be followed by a group game that involves all performers. Characters and themes are introduced and then recur in a series of connected scenes; with each beat the three scenes return and by the end the three scenes have converged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening (suggestion and premise extraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a suggestion from the audience that is dissected for premises in an opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openings include techniques such as the pattern game, the invocation, or a monologue. The opening generates material and premises that seed the scenes and recurring games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble size
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical cast size for a Harold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This long-form is typically performed by a six to nine improvisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: First beat: three distinct two-person scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The first beat typically consists of three two-person scenes that are all distinct and are not connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These scenes are separate setups which will be returned to in later beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second beat: repeat and explore games
rubrics_metrics.description: The second beat repeats each scene from the first beat and further explores the 'games' found in those previous scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the second beat to develop and heighten the comedic games or patterns introduced in each first-beat scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third beat: heightening and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: The third beat continues to further heighten the games from the previous beats; scenes should be shorter than in previous beats and may connect to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the third beat, improvisors may make connections between the scenes by incorporating characters or elements from other scenes. Ideally, the third beat is a single scene which incorporates all three games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group game between beats
rubrics_metrics.description: A group game follows each beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each group game should involve all performers and serves as a transition and ensemble moment between beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence of characters and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce characters and themes early so they can recur through the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters/themes introduced in openings and first-beat scenes should reappear and be developed across beats to allow convergence and payoff by the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-wheels Harold (three-act teaching variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simplified Harold structure described as three acts (or 'beats'), each with three scenes and a group segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With each beat the three scenes return; the training-wheels Harold is used for learning the form and emphasizes convergence by the end of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modified Harold variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Harolds with added requirements or constraints that change the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: Monoscene (Harold set in one location), Sybil (Harold performed by a solo performer), The Bat (Harold performed in the dark), and The Armando (Harold with a guest monologist telling true stories). Each variant preserves Harold principles while imposing its specific constraint.
